extracted.intended_audience: travelers and ethnographers conducting fieldwork in West Africa (collectors of folklore/fetish/ju-ju material)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical methodological guidance for collecting, recording, and interpreting West African 'fetish' beliefs, stories, and language data during fieldwork; emphasizes preparation, language, context, and mindset. Targets on-the-ground collectors and student ethnologists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology caution: 'fetish' and 'ju-ju'
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither 'fetish' nor 'ju-ju' are native words; 'fetish' comes from Portuguese 'Feitico' and 'ju-ju' from the French word for a toy or doll.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these conventional terms with awareness of their origins and limits — 'fetish' is preferable because the native image functions more like the image of a saint (a residence/haunt of a spirit) than a toy. Make explicit in reports that these are outsider labels, not native terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware missionary/Christian contamination of traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: In places with missionary influence natives either conceal things they fear will bring them into derision, or possess traditions of Christian origin altered by the African mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess degree of missionary contact before treating a variant as 'authentic.' Treat stories that seem to mirror Christian parables with special caution and investigate possible origins or syncretism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and study 'trade English' thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade English is widely diffused as an intercommunication language; it is a definite structure with peculiar verb forms and no genders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume it is 'broken' English; study its idioms and literal forms (example: 'Yes, sah' may mean 'yes, I have not cleaned the lamp'). Learn through immersion (listen to seasoned contacts such as a second mate) and by studying exemplar texts (the appended letter is given as a 'highest style' example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ostentatious symbols of your religion or authority
rubrics_metrics.description: "If you go hunting the African idea with the flag of your own religion or opinions floating ostentatiously over you, you will similarly get a very poor bag."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not display banners, flags, or overt symbols of your state/religion/opinion in the field; such displays change indigenous behaviour and degrade the quality of your data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach without doctrinaire preconceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Burn all your notions about sun-myths and the fashionable idea that dreams gave humans first notion of the soul; Frazer's Golden Bough is useful but not a universal key.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of grand universal theories as explanatory shortcuts. Read the ethnological literature to inform yourself, but keep your mind open and let the facts lead. Avoid imposing theoretical frameworks rigidly on field data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare with broad ethnological reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended background: Tylor's Primitive Culture, Westermarck on Human Marriage, Waitz, Topinard, A. B. Ellis's works, Burton, Pliny, and as much Aristotle as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this preparatory reading to sharpen comparative judgement and to recognize recurring motifs, but not to force-fit local phenomena into preconceived schemas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make your mind pliant to native thought-forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The difficulty of the language is far less than the difficulties with your own mind. Unless you can make it pliant enough to follow the African idea step by step you will not bag your game.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop mental flexibility: resist assuming natives think like you, follow local logic patiently, and be prepared for different categories, emphases, and narrative styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid intrusive or insulting field practices (e.g., skull/chest measurements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attempt to measure people's skulls and chests as this will get you disliked by blacks or whites alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from physical anthropometry or other intrusive activities that offend subjects and jeopardize rapport; prioritize ethical, respectful methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record original material contemporaneously and precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: You must always have your original material—carefully noted down at the time of occurrence—with you, so that you may answer 'Why?' with concrete evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take careful, contemporaneous field notes; preserve raw texts and transcriptions as primary evidence. These originals are indispensable for later analysis and for defending interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ticket and contextualize every collected item
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring home these things in their raw state, but ticket them with the culture of the tribe they belonged to, the conditions it lives under, locality, and so forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attach explicit metadata to each item: tribe, village, speaker, date/time, social context, elicitation circumstances, and any environmental or missionary influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect multi-thematic stories and regional variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Very few African stories bear on one subject alone, and they hardly ever stick to a point; many variants exist across places (same legend heard in multiple locales).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect multiple variants, note locality differences, and avoid over-interpretation of single tellings. Comparative collection across sites is essential to understand variant structure and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exemplar study and apprenticeship methods for language learning
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the best ways of learning trade English is to listen to a seasoned second mate regulating loading/unloading, and to study high-style examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn through listening to skilled communicators and by copying exemplars; combine immersion with targeted study of well-formed examples to master idioms and register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult established thinkers for interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Lay the results of your collection before some great thinker and he will write upon it the opinion that his greater and clearer vision makes him more fit to form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After collecting and annotating raw data, seek peer review and mentorship from experienced ethnologists to refine analysis and place findings in comparative context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and note syncretism and story migration
rubrics_metrics.description: Some local tales may be modified versions of foreign (e.g., Christian) parables; the same legend may be told across Fernando Po, Calabar, and Gaboon in variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace possible sources and transmission routes for tales; when encountering a version that resembles non-local material, document diffusion clues (e.g., missionary presence, trade links).
